entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen30482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30483" type="x-p"/> O, do not this abominable thing - A strong specimen of affectionate entreaty. One of the finest figures of poetry, when judiciously managed, the anthropopathia, the ascribing human passions to God, is often used by this prophet: so God is said to grieve, to mourn, to have his bowels moved with compassion, to repent, to be angry, etc. Here he is represented as tenderly expostulating: O, do not; or, I entreat you, do not that abominable thing which I hate. <div eID="gen30483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30484" type="x-p"/> 1. Do it not: your God commands. <div eID="gen30484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30485" type="x-p"/> 2. O, do it not: your Father entreats. <div eID="gen30485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30486" type="x-p"/> 3. It is an abominable thing, and should not be done. <div eID="gen30486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30487" type="x-p"/> 4. I hate it, and on that account ye should abstain from it.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen30492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30493" type="x-p"/> This great evil against your souls - Will not self-interest weigh with you? See what ruin your conduct has brought upon your country. Your fathers sinned as you are doing; and where are they now? Either destroyed, or in captivity. And you are now taking the same way to your own destruction.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen30495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30496" type="x-p"/> And when we burned incense to the queen of heaven - The Moon seems to have been called מלכת melecheth, as the sun was called מלך molech. The Hindoos pour out water to the sun thrice a day; and to the moon whenever they worship her. <div eID="gen30496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30497" type="x-p"/> The idolatrous worship of these people was a sort of imitation of the worship of the true God; only sacrifice was not common in it. The factious women here tell us in what it consisted. <div eID="gen30497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30498" type="x-p"/> 1. They burnt incense to the moon, and perhaps to the sun and the planets. <div eID="gen30498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30499" type="x-p"/> 2. They poured out libations to her. <div eID="gen30499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30500" type="x-p"/> 3. They made and consecrated cakes to her. <div eID="gen30500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30501" type="x-p"/> All these were prescribed in the worship of the true God. See, among others, <reference osisRef="Exo.29.23">Exo 29:23</reference>, etc.; <reference osisRef="Lev.2.4">Lev 2:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.23.16">Lev 23:16</reference>; and <reference osisRef="Num.6.15">Num 6:15</reference>. And the women vindicate their conduct by asserting that they did all this by the consent of their husbands: "Did we worship her without our men?"

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen30501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30502" type="x-p"/> Therefore is your land a desolation - I grant that ye and your husbands have joined together in these abominations; and what is the consequence? "The Lord could no longer bear because of your evil doings; and therefore is your land a desolation, and an astonishment, and a curse, without an inhabitant, this day."

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen30502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30503" type="x-p"/> Behold I will give Pharaoh-hophra - That is, Pharaoh Apries. How this and the prophecies in the preceding chapter were fulfilled, we learn from ancient historians. The sum of such information is this: the subjects of Pharaoh Apries rebelling, he sent Amasis, one of his generals, to reduce them to their duty. But no sooner had Amasis begun to make his speech, than they fixed a helmet on his head, and proclaimed him king. Amasis accepted the title, and confirmed the Egyptians in their revolt; and the greater part of the nation declaring for him, Apries was obliged to retire into Upper Egypt; and the country being thus weakened by intestine war, was attacked and easily overcome by Nebuchadnezzar, who on quitting it left Amasis his viceroy. After Nebuchadnezzar's departure, Apries marched against Amasis; but, being defeated at Memphis, was taken prisoner, carried to Sais, and was strangled in his own palace, thus verifying this prophecy. See Herodotus in Euterpe. <div eID="gen30503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30504" type="x-p"/> Thus Nebuchadnezzar made an easy conquest of the land. He conquered it as easily as "a shepherd puts on his cloak: he went thence in peace," having clothed himself with its spoils; and left all quiet under a viceroy of his own choosing. The rebellion of Pharaoh's subjects was the "fire that God kindled in Egypt," <reference osisRef="Jer.43.12">Jer 43:12</reference>. And thus was he "delivered into the hands of his enemies," his revolted people; and "into the hand of him who sought his life," i.e., Amasis his general. And thus the whole prophecy was literally fulfilled.  <chapter eID="Jer.44"/> <div eID="gen30504" type="x-p"/>
